On Port-Hamiltonian Formulation of Hysteretic
Energy Storage Elements: The Backlash Case
J.R. Keulen, B. Jayawardhana, A.J. van der Schaft
Abstract— This paper presents a port-Hamiltonian for-
mulation of hysteretic energy storage elements. First, we
revisit the passivity property of backlash-driven storage
elements by presenting a family of storage functions as-
sociated to the dissipativity property of such elements. We
explicitly derive the corresponding available storage and
required supply functions `a la Willems [1], and show the
interlacing property of the aforementioned family of storage
functions sandwiched between the available storage and
required supply functions. Second, using the proposed
family of storage functions, we present a port-Hamiltonian
formulation of hysteretic inductors as prototypical storage
elements in port-Hamiltonian systems. In particular, we
show how a Hamiltonian function can be chosen from the
family of storage functions and how the hysteretic ele-
ments can be expressed as port-Hamiltonian system with
feedthrough term, where the feedthrough term represents
energy dissipation. Correspondingly, we illustrate its ap-
plicability in describing an RLC circuit (in parallel and in
series) containing a hysteretic inductor element.
Index Terms— Hysteresis; Dissipative Systems; Back-
lash; Port-Hamiltonian Systems; Nonlinear RLC Circuits;
Passivity.
I. INTRODUCTION
MODERN high-precision technology increasingly op-
erates at the nano- and microscale. At these scales,
hysteresis is a fundamental limiting factor for system perfor-
mance, stability and efficiency. Hysteresis is a phenomenon
where the current state does not only depend on the current
input, but also on the history of previous inputs. Such behavior
is encountered in a wide spectrum of physical systems that
contain ferromagnetic-, piezoelectric materials, magnetostric-
tive actuators, shape-memory alloys, etc. [2], [3]. In ther-
modynamics and in electro-mechanical systems, the presence
of hysteresis loop is always associated to energy dissipation,
where the enclosed area of a hysteresis loop represents the
dissipated energy per cycle. Over the past decades, accurate
modeling of hysteresis phenomena has been investigated for

[4]–[6].
Several mathematical frameworks have been proposed to
describe hysteresis, including operator-based models such as
the Preisach and Prandtl-Ishlinskii (PI) models [2], and differ-
ential equation-based models such as the Duhem models [7].
The backlash operator, also the fundamental building block of
the PI model, belongs to a subfamily of Duhem operators with
counterclockwise input-output dynamics [8], [9], a property
that is connected to passivity in [10], where it is shown that
hysteretic systems do not generate energy but dissipate it over
each cycle. In the dissipativity framework of Willems [1], a
system is dissipative if there exists a storage function satisfying
a dissipation inequality with a given supply-rate function.
For hysteretic systems, the characterization of such storage
functions is non-trivial due to the path-dependent, multivalued
nature of the input-output map, where a single input value may
correspond to multiple outputs. While passivity of the backlash
operator has been established [11], an explicit characterization
of the family of admissible storage functions, bounded by the
available storage and required supply functions, has not been
addressed in the literature. Moreover, the non-conservative
nature of hysteresis makes the unified formulation into an
energy-based framework such as port-Hamiltonian systems
particularly challenging.
Port-Hamiltonian (pH) systems provide a structured,
energy-based, modeling framework that has proven effective
for physical systems across multiple domains [12], [13].
However, physical elements exhibiting hysteresis behavior
cannot be represented by a single storage port and dissipa-
tion port alone [13]. In [14], [15], hysteretic systems are
modeled by introducing an additional nonlinear dissipative
element to capture hysteretic energy dissipation. In recent
years, irreversible pH formulations have been proposed [16],
where the dissipated energy is accounted for as thermal energy
(entropy). A modular passivity based pH of piezo actuators
has been proposed in [17], using ’hysterons’ as in [15] to
capture the hysteretic behavior. Nevertheless, a systematic pH
formulation that directly incorporates hysteretic dissipation
through a nonlinear potential, consistent with the Willems
dissipativity framework, remains an open problem.
In this paper, we address these challenges by developing
a pH formulation of the backlash-driven storage elements.
By considering the backlash hysteretic phenomenon in aarXiv:2603.25211v2  [eess.SY]  27 Mar 2026

nonlinear inductor element, we present a family of storage
functions which are sandwiched between the available storage
and required supply functions in the sense of Willems [1].
Based on these results, we show how to define an appropriate
Hamiltonian function that allows us to cast the nonlinear in-
ductor into a general port-Hamiltonian formalism that includes
feedthrough terms. Accordingly, we show how we can include
this hysteretic inductor element to represent an interconnected
RLC circuit via the general pH formalism.

IV. PORT-HAMILTONIAN FORMULATION
In this section, we first derive a port-Hamiltonian (pH) rep-
resentation of the backlash inductor element. For illustration
purpose, we present its interconnection with a linear resistor
and linear capacitor in series and in parallel.
A. Backlash inductor element in pH

in Fig. 1. Using the multivalued sign mapping as in (1), a

V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have shown that the backlash inductor
element admits a family of storage functions that are lower-
bounded by the available storage and upper-bounded by the
required supply, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The backlash inductor
element can then be expressed in a pH framework with a
nonlinear dissipation feedthrough term, allowing the system to
be written in standard nonlinear pH form, while preserving the
skew-symmetric interconnection structure and energy balance.
The formulation is subsequently extended to both parallel and
series RC network configurations incorporating the backlash
inductor. For the resulting network, passivity with respect to
the supply rate is established using the total Hamiltonian. The
generalization of the pH modeling of the backlash storage
elements to other hysteretic storage elements using complex
hysteresis operators, such as nonlinear backlash, Preisach or
Duhem models, will be reported in our future works.REFERENCES

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document focuses on the port-Hamiltonian formulation of hysteretic energy storage elements, specifically addressing the backlash case. The main points covered are:

*   **Passivity of Backlash-Driven Storage Elements:** The paper revisits and presents a family of storage functions associated with the dissipativity property of backlash-driven storage elements.
*   **Explicit Derivation of Available Storage and Required Supply:** The authors explicitly derive the available storage and required supply functions for these elements, following Willems' framework. They also demonstrate the interlacing property of the proposed storage functions between these bounds.
*   **Port-Hamiltonian Formulation of Hysteretic Inductors:** Using the derived family of storage functions, the paper presents a port-Hamiltonian formulation for hysteretic inductors as prototypical storage elements.
*   **Hamiltonian Function Selection and Feedthrough Term:** It is shown how to select a Hamiltonian function from the family and express hysteretic elements as port-Hamiltonian systems with a feedthrough term, which represents energy dissipation.
*   **Application to RLC Circuits:** The applicability of this formulation is illustrated by describing RLC circuits (both parallel and series) containing a hysteretic inductor element.
*   **Motivation and Background:** The introduction highlights the importance of hysteresis in modern high-precision technology, its association with energy dissipation, and the challenges in modeling it within existing frameworks like port-Hamiltonian systems. It also reviews existing mathematical frameworks for hysteresis and the limitations of current port-Hamiltonian approaches.
*   **Preliminaries on Dissipativity and Port-Hamiltonian Systems:** The document includes preliminary sections defining dissipativity theory (including storage functions, available storage, and required supply) and the general form of port-Hamiltonian systems with nonlinear dissipation.

structure.title: PRELIMINARIES
structure.summary:
This partial document focuses on representing nonlinear inductor elements, particularly those exhibiting hysteresis, within the port-Hamiltonian (pH) formalism. The main points covered are:

*   **Storage Functions for Nonlinear Inductors:** The document introduces a family of storage functions for nonlinear inductor elements. These functions are bounded by "available storage" and "required supply" functions, concepts derived from Willems' work on dissipativity.
*   **Hamiltonian Formulation:** It demonstrates how to define an appropriate Hamiltonian function for these nonlinear inductors. This allows them to be incorporated into a general port-Hamiltonian framework, including feedthrough terms.
*   **Interconnected Systems:** The document shows how this hysteretic inductor element can be used to represent interconnected RLC circuits within the general pH formalism.
*   **Dissipativity Theory Preliminaries:** A section provides background on dissipativity theory, defining supply rates, storage functions, and the dissipation inequality. It also introduces the concepts of available storage and required supply as bounds for admissible storage functions.
*   **Port-Hamiltonian Systems Preliminaries:** Another section outlines the general form of port-Hamiltonian systems, including their state-space representation, interconnection matrices, and dissipation potential, highlighting how the Hamiltonian acts as a storage function.
*   **Passivity of Hysteretic Storage Elements:** The document specifically addresses the passivity of backlash-driven storage elements, with a focus on nonlinear inductors. It details how to derive the associated available storage and required supply functions for these hysteretic elements.
*   **Backlash Inductor Example:** A concrete example of a backlash inductor element evolving in the (current, magnetic flux) plane is presented, illustrating its coupling to physical equations and port variables.

nodes.title: Port-Hamiltonian systems
nodes.summary: This partial document focuses on modeling nonlinear inductor elements with hysteresis using the port-Hamiltonian formalism. It introduces a family of storage functions for such elements, bounded by "available storage" and "required supply" functions as defined by Willems. The document then demonstrates how to define an appropriate Hamiltonian function to represent the hysteretic inductor within a general port-Hamiltonian framework, including feedthrough terms. This allows for the inclusion of these hysteretic inductors in interconnected RLC circuits. The preliminary sections define dissipativity theory, including passive systems, and the general form of port-Hamiltonian systems. The core of the document presents a specific proposition for storage functions of a backlash inductor and proves its properties, including monotonicity with respect to a parameter that characterizes the hysteresis.

structure.title: PASSIVITY OF BACKLASH-DRIVEN STORAGE ELEMENTS
structure.summary: The document discusses the modeling and analysis of a backlash inductor, which exhibits hysteresis behavior similar to inductors with ferromagnetic cores. It introduces a family of admissible storage functions for the backlash operator and proves their properties, including monotonicity with respect to a parameter $\gamma$. The document then defines and derives the available storage function ($S_a$) and the required supply function ($S_r$) for the backlash inductor, which represent the maximum extractable energy and minimum required energy, respectively. These functions are shown to be the extremal elements of the family of storage functions. Finally, the document presents a port-Hamiltonian formulation for the backlash inductor, highlighting its passive nature and its analogy to Coulomb friction. It also outlines the port-Hamiltonian representation of an RLC network incorporating the backlash inductor in both series and parallel configurations.

structure.title: PORT-HAMILTONIAN FORMULATION
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the port-Hamiltonian (pH) formulation of a backlash inductor element and its interconnection with linear circuit components.

The main points covered are:

*   **Optimal Trajectory and Dissipation:** It discusses the concept of an optimal trajectory for minimizing energy supply, highlighting that non-monotone trajectories introduce additional dissipation.
*   **Storage Function Bounds:** It defines bounds for an admissible storage function, denoted as $S_a(I, \phi)$ and $S_r(I, \phi)$, which are extremal elements of a family of functions.
*   **Port-Hamiltonian Representation of Backlash Inductor:** It derives a pH representation for the backlash inductor element using a multivalued sign mapping and a Hamiltonian $H_{bf}(\phi) = \frac{1}{2L}\phi^2$.
*   **Dissipation Mechanism:** It explains that the backlash introduces energy dissipation through a nonlinear feedthrough term, analogous to Coulomb friction, rather than directly in the state equation.
*   **Passivity:** It demonstrates that the backlash inductor is passive with respect to its port variables $(V, I)$.
*   **Convex Analysis Formulation:** It rewrites the pH model using convex analysis, expressing the multivalued mapping as the sub-differential of a convex function $P(V) = \frac{h_L}{L}|V|$.
*   **RC Network with Backlash Inductor:** It outlines the derivation of the pH formulation for an RLC network comprising a backlash inductor, a resistor, and a capacitor, considering both series and parallel interconnection configurations.
*   **Total Hamiltonian:** It defines the total Hamiltonian for the network as the sum of the backlash inductor's Hamiltonian and the capacitor's energy storage.
*   **Parallel Interconnection pH Formulation:** It presents the specific pH formulation for the parallel interconnection of the backlash inductor, resistor, and capacitor, identifying the system matrices $(J, G, M)$.

nodes.title: RC network with backlash ferromagnet inductor
nodes.summary:
The document discusses the port-Hamiltonian (pH) formulation of a backlash inductor element and its interconnection with RLC networks. Key points include:

*   **Backlash Inductor Modeling:** The backlash inductor is characterized by a hysteretic dissipation term that acts as a nonlinear feedthrough mapping, analogous to Coulomb friction. This dissipation is structurally different from typical nonlinear dissipation elements.
*   **Storage Functions:** The backlash inductor admits a family of storage functions bounded by available storage and required supply.
*   **Port-Hamiltonian Representation:** The backlash inductor is represented in a pH framework, allowing it to be written in a standard nonlinear pH form while preserving energy balance and interconnection structure. This formulation utilizes convex analysis and sub-differential mappings.
*   **RC Network Interconnections:** The pH formulation is extended to series and parallel interconnections of the backlash inductor with linear resistors and capacitors.
*   **Passivity Analysis:** The RLC networks incorporating the backlash inductor are shown to be passive with respect to the supply rate, with energy dissipation attributed to both resistive and hysteretic losses.
*   **Future Work:** The authors plan to generalize this pH modeling approach to other hysteretic storage elements using complex hysteresis operators.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the energy balance and passivity of RLC networks incorporating a backlash inductor element. It analyzes both parallel and series configurations of these networks, demonstrating how the backlash inductor introduces hysteretic losses. The document utilizes a port-Hamiltonian (pH) framework to model these systems, showing that despite the rate-independent nature of the hysteresis, the standard pH power balance and passivity properties are preserved. The conclusion summarizes the successful application of the pH framework to model backlash inductors and their extension to RC networks, establishing passivity with respect to the supply rate. Future work is mentioned regarding the generalization of this modeling approach to other hysteretic storage elements.
